    tensorlake NPM package compromised with Shai Hulud worm
    aikido.dev · 08 Oct 2026 03:32 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSblockchain-dead-dropbuncargoethereumgithubhackbrowserdataiseekaigogonpmnpm-preinstall-scriptpypishai-huludtensorlake
    In plain words

    A malicious version of the tensorlake software package was placed on npm, a service developers use to download code; the affected version is 0.5.144. Anyone who installed it may have had passwords, cloud access keys, cryptocurrency wallet information, and other private data copied from their computer, while the malicious code also tried to spread into other software projects. This matters because a single compromised developer computer can expose an organization’s systems and customers, so affected users should consider their stored credentials unsafe and replace them immediately.

    Summary
    The npm package tensorlake version 0.5.144 was compromised with a Shai-Hulud worm that steals credentials and browser wallet data, spreads through supply chains, and can wipe infected systems if its GitHub token is revoked. Organizations that installed this version should treat affected hosts as fully compromised, remove it, and immediately rotate exposed secrets.

    On 8 October 2026, a threat actor published tensorlake version 0.5.144 to npm with a variant of the Shai-Hulud worm. Tensorlake is a serverless sandbox for AI agents with more than 100,000 reported lifetime npm installs. The article reports no evidence that the actor published compromised versions of Tensorlake’s PyPI or Cargo packages.

    The malicious package runs a preinstall script that launches obfuscated code through the Bun runtime. It attempts to steal sensitive environment variables, local credential files, browser data, and data from 14 cryptocurrency wallet browser extensions, while also attempting to replicate through connected supply chains. It uses the hardcoded domain iseekaigogo[.]com and an Ethereum-contract-based mechanism for command-and-control information, and it includes a dead-man’s switch that can wipe infected systems if an embedded GitHub token is revoked.

    The malicious files were introduced into the Tensorlake GitHub repository through verified commits made under a maintainer identity on 7 October 2026. The repository was compromised for approximately 20 hours before the npm publication occurred. The article advises treating infected systems as fully compromised and urgently rotating all secrets and credentials they contained.

    • The malware includes a dead-man’s switch that can wipe infected machines if its embedded GitHub token is revoked, making investigation and containment more urgent.
    • Although the malware can retrieve an alternate command-and-control address through an Ethereum contract, the contract’s most recent value was the same hardcoded domain, iseekaigogo[.]com.
    • The payload targets browser storage for 14 cryptocurrency wallet extensions and downloads a system-specific HackBrowserData tool, extending its collection beyond typical development and cloud credentials.
    • A tensorlake-specific WORMTAG marker suggests this was a new compromise rather than continued reinfection from an earlier Shai-Hulud wave.
    • The attacker introduced the malicious files through verified maintainer commits and controlled the repository for about 20 hours before successfully publishing the npm package.
    Key Points
    • 01A compromised version of the tensorlake npm package, version 0.5.144, was published on 8 October 2026 and contains a variant of the Shai-Hulud worm.
    • 02The malicious package runs through a preinstall script that drops the Bun runtime and executes an obfuscated payload in lib/Math_Symbol.js.
    • 03The payload attempts to collect sensitive environment variables, local credential files, browser data, and data from 14 cryptocurrency browser extensions.
    • 04The malware uses iseekaigogo[.]com as a hardcoded command-and-control address and can retrieve an alternative address through a threat actor-controlled Ethereum contract.
    • 05The article advises treating infected systems as fully compromised and rotating all secrets and credentials they contained as a critical priority.
    OPEN SOURCE ↗
    JUSTIFICATION

    This reports an active npm supply-chain compromise affecting tensorlake version 0.5.144, with credential theft, browser wallet targeting, self-propagation attempts, and a destructive wipe mechanism. Security teams and developers that may have installed the package need immediate incident response and credential rotation.

    Tensorlake npm Package Compromised: A Worm With a Hostage Token That Wipes Your Machine If You Revoke It
    stepsecurity.io · 08 Oct 2026 03:19 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
    TAGSbunclaude-codegh-token-monitorgithubiseekaigogo-comnpmshai-huludstepsecuritytensorlakevisual-studio-code
    In plain words

    A harmful update to the Tensorlake software package, version 0.5.144, can steal passwords, account access codes, cloud keys, and other sensitive information from developers’ computers when they install it. It can also use stolen access to copy itself into other software projects and set up files that run again when a project is opened in common coding tools. People who installed the affected version, or used the compromised Tensorlake source code, need to remove its monitoring program before canceling stolen GitHub access codes, because canceling them first may cause it to erase the files in their home folder. This matters because one tampered software update can spread from a single developer’s computer into many projects and expose many organizations’ accounts and secrets.

    Summary
    The npm package tensorlake@0.5.144 was compromised with a credential-stealing worm that spreads through npm and GitHub and installs a token-monitoring persistence mechanism that can wipe a victim’s home directory if its stolen GitHub token is revoked. Affected users should first disable and remove the gh-token-monitor service, then rotate all exposed credentials and pin Tensorlake to 0.5.143.

    tensorlake@0.5.144 on npm was released with malicious code that runs during installation on developer machines. The package steals GitHub and npm tokens, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, browser logins, and configuration for AI coding tools. It encrypts and sends collected data to a public GitHub repository created in the victim’s account or to iseekaigogo.com.

    The malware can use stolen npm tokens to infect and republish a victim’s packages, and stolen GitHub tokens to add files that run when repositories are opened in Claude Code or Visual Studio Code. It also installs a gh-token-monitor service that checks a stolen GitHub token every minute and deletes the user’s home directory if the token is revoked or otherwise rejected. Affected users are instructed to remove this monitor before revoking credentials, then rotate exposed secrets and pin Tensorlake to version 0.5.143.

    • The compromised release had a valid npm provenance attestation because it was published from the legitimate repository, showing that provenance identifies where a package was built rather than whether its code is safe.
    • The install hook skips CI environments, indicating that developer workstations—not automated build systems—are the primary target, although CI secrets should still be rotated if they were accessible.
    • Revoking the stolen GitHub token is unsafe until the gh-token-monitor persistence mechanism is removed, because the monitor is designed to erase the user’s home directory when the token becomes invalid.
    • The malware can persist beyond the initial package installation by placing configuration files in repositories that trigger when developers open them in Claude Code or Visual Studio Code.
    • The malicious commits were pushed directly to the Tensorlake main branch without pull requests, and the package release was subsequently published through the repository’s normal release workflow.
    Key Points
    • 01The npm package tensorlake@0.5.144 contains a malicious preinstall script that targets developer machines, downloads Bun, and runs an obfuscated file.
    • 02The malicious code steals GitHub and npm tokens, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, browser logins, and AI-tool configuration, then sends encrypted data to a GitHub repository it creates or to iseekaigogo.com.
    • 03Using stolen npm and GitHub tokens, the malware can republish infected packages and add persistent .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json files to repositories it can access.
    • 04The malware installs a gh-token-monitor service that checks a stolen GitHub token every minute and deletes the user’s home directory if GitHub rejects the token.
    • 05Affected users should remove the gh-token-monitor service before revoking credentials, then rotate exposed secrets and pin Tensorlake to version 0.5.143.
    OPEN SOURCE ↗
    JUSTIFICATION

    This is a specific, active software supply-chain compromise involving a published npm package that steals high-value credentials, self-propagates through victims’ npm and GitHub access, and persists through developer tools. Its token-revocation-triggered home-directory deletion mechanism makes the remediation sequence immediately safety-critical for potentially affected users.

    In plain words

    A downloaded version of Tensorlake’s developer software package was secretly altered to steal passwords, access keys, and other sensitive information from computers where it was installed. It can target accounts and data used with services such as GitHub, Amazon Web Services, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, cryptocurrency wallets, and several AI coding tools, and may keep running even after the package is removed. This matters because the malicious code can spread through other software packages, putting additional developers and organizations at risk; anyone who installed version 0.5.144 is advised to remove it and change their credentials.

    Summary
    Tensorlake’s npm SDK version 0.5.144 was compromised with the Shai-Hulud self-propagating credential-stealing worm, which can steal cloud, source-control, Kubernetes, Vault, SSH, and AI-tool secrets while establishing persistence. Users who installed the malicious release should remove it immediately, investigate affected environments, and rotate all potentially exposed credentials.

    The Tensorlake TypeScript SDK package on npm was compromised as part of the ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack. Malicious version 0.5.144 contained obfuscated code that steals credentials, sends out collected data, establishes persistence, and can execute code supplied by attackers. The version is no longer available from npm, and users who installed it are advised to remove it and rotate credentials.

    The malicious package uses a preinstall hook to launch an obfuscated loader and a Bun-based credential-stealing, self-propagating worm. It targets npm and GitHub tokens, AWS secrets, Vault and Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, .env files, cryptocurrency wallets, messaging data, and files associated with Claude, Cursor, Kiro, Windsurf, and Zed. It can also republish compromised packages through a victim’s publishing identity, plant GitHub Actions workflows, and write files that cause it to run again when repositories are opened in Claude Code or Visual Studio Code.

    • Removing the affected dependency alone may not end the risk, because the malware can establish persistence that retains attacker access after the package is removed.
    • The malware includes a “hostage token” mechanism that monitors whether a stolen GitHub token remains valid and, if it is revoked, can run attacker-supplied PowerShell code through Invoke-Expression.
    • Rather than relying on only one server for instructions, the malware resolves its command-and-control address through an Ethereum contract and can use GitHub as a fallback location for stolen data.
    • The malware writes settings and task files into accessible repositories so that it can run again when someone opens those projects in Claude Code or Visual Studio Code.
    Key Points
    • 01Tensorlake npm package version 0.5.144 was compromised as part of the ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud software supply-chain campaign and has been removed from the npm registry.
    • 02The malicious release uses a preinstall script and obfuscated Bun-based code to run a credential-stealing, self-propagating worm.
    • 03The malware targets npm and GitHub tokens, AWS credentials, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, .env files, cryptocurrency wallets, messaging-app data, and configuration files for several AI coding tools.
    • 04The worm can republish compromised package versions using a victim’s publishing identity and may plant GitHub Actions workflows, while also creating files that run when repositories are opened in Claude Code or Visual Studio Code.
    • 05Users who installed the malicious version are advised to remove it immediately and rotate their credentials.
    OPEN SOURCE ↗
    JUSTIFICATION

    This reports a concrete npm supply-chain compromise delivering a self-propagating credential-stealing worm with persistence and remote-code execution capabilities. It is especially relevant to organizations using Tensorlake version 0.5.144 or npm publishing, GitHub, cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, and AI development tooling credentials.

In plain words

A harmful version of Tensorlake’s software package was placed on npm, a service developers use to download code, and it could run automatically when installed. It was designed to steal passwords, access keys, and other private information from developers’ computers and company build systems, then give attackers ongoing access. People and organizations that installed version 0.5.144 may be affected, including teams using Tensorlake to build AI tools. This matters because even software meant to safely run AI-generated code can expose valuable company accounts and deployment systems before that safety layer is ever used.

Summary
Tensorlake’s npm SDK version 0.5.144 was compromised with the Shai-Hulud/ChainDrop credential-stealing worm, which runs during installation via a preinstall hook and can steal secrets, establish persistence, and spread through npm. Organizations that installed it should treat affected hosts as compromised, remove persistence before revoking tokens, and rebuild systems from trusted sources.

Tensorlake’s npm SDK version 0.5.144 was compromised in a ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud supply-chain attack. Published on October 8, 2026, the release contained obfuscated malware and was flagged by Socket about 11 minutes later. The malicious package used a preinstall hook, meaning its code could run during installation without a developer importing the SDK or starting an AI agent.

The payload targets credentials and sensitive data from npm, GitHub, AWS, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, SSH keys, environment files, cryptocurrency wallets, messaging applications, and AI development tools. It can send collected data to attackers, establish persistent access, execute remotely supplied code, and use stolen npm publishing credentials to spread to other packages. Its remote endpoint is resolved through an Ethereum contract using public RPC endpoints, with a GitHub fallback.

Organizations that installed tensorlake@0.5.144 should treat hosts where the installation script ran as compromised. The article advises blocking the version, isolating affected systems, investigating persistence, and removing the gh-token-monitor before revoking GitHub tokens because revocation can trigger an attacker-supplied handler intended to wipe the user’s home directory. Teams should then replace exposed credentials, audit connected accounts for unauthorized activity, and rebuild affected environments from trusted sources.

  • Installing the compromised SDK was sufficient for exposure because its preinstall hook ran before developers imported the package or used any AI agent functionality.
  • The package’s use in AI-agent infrastructure does not protect the installation environment: the malicious code runs on the developer workstation, server, or build runner before any generated code reaches Tensorlake’s isolated sandbox.
  • The remote control endpoint was not hardcoded; the payload resolved it through an Ethereum contract using public RPC services, with a GitHub fallback.
  • Revoking a stolen GitHub token before removing the persistent gh-token-monitor can trigger attacker-supplied code intended to wipe the affected user’s home directory.
  • The reported 12,000 weekly downloads reflect the package’s overall usage and do not establish how many times the malicious release was downloaded or how many systems were infected.
Key Points
  • 01Tensorlake npm SDK version 0.5.144, published on October 8, 2026, contained obfuscated malicious code associated with the ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud supply-chain campaign.
  • 02A preinstall script ran the malicious loader during package installation, so the code could execute without a developer importing the SDK or starting an agent.
  • 03The payload targeted npm and GitHub tokens, AWS and Kubernetes credentials, HashiCorp Vault, SSH keys, environment files, cryptocurrency wallets, messaging-app data, and AI development-tool configuration files.
  • 04The malware could exfiltrate collected secrets, establish persistence, execute attacker-supplied code, and use stolen npm publishing credentials to spread to additional packages.
  • 05Organizations that installed tensorlake@0.5.144 are advised to isolate affected hosts, remove the gh-token-monitor persistence mechanism before revoking tokens, rotate exposed credentials, and rebuild affected environments from trusted sources.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific supply-chain compromise in an npm package that can execute malicious code automatically during installation and steal a broad range of credentials. Organizations that installed tensorlake@0.5.144 face immediate incident-response needs, including persistence removal before token revocation.

Japan Sees Sharp Rise in Web Data Leaks Amid Mobile API Abuse and Metabase Attacks
thehackernews.com · 08 Oct 2026 15:45 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSapi-key-theftblind-nosql-injectioncisacve-2026-72898francejapanjpcert-ccmacnicametabasemonogatari-corporationpark24personal-information-protection-commissionpolandsouth-koreasql-injection
93
In plain words

Japanese authorities are warning about a sharp rise in cases where outsiders obtained personal information from websites, apps, and internal business tools that were accidentally reachable from the internet. Recent victims include a car-sharing service and a restaurant chain, with millions of customer records and, in some cases, identity-document images exposed. The incidents show that attackers can misuse hidden app connections, weak account protections, or unpatched software to reach data, putting people at risk when organizations keep large amounts of personal information online.

Summary
JPCERT/CC warns that a surge of Japanese personal-data leaks is linked to mobile-app API abuse, weak access controls and exploitation of the critical Metabase SQL injection flaw CVE-2026-72898. Organizations should urgently patch Metabase, review logs and API permissions, rotate exposed credentials, and enforce rate limits and least privilege.

JPCERT/CC warned of a series of personal-data leaks affecting Japanese organizations, where attackers have abused mobile-app APIs and targeted known software flaws. The incidents have affected consumer apps, business intelligence tools, and employee-facing management systems that were not expected to be publicly accessible. JPCERT/CC said its information is limited and fragmentary, did not name any attacker or victim, and cautioned that the same method may not have been used in every case.

Macnica counted 119 similar publicly disclosed web-system incidents in Japan through October 6, 2026, compared with 84 during all of 2025 and 62 in 2024; 81 of this year’s cases were disclosed from July onward. Park24 said data from about 6.6 million Times Car accounts was obtained, including identity-document images from about 1.6 million accounts, while Monogatari Corporation reported 10,788,963 leaked records from the Yakiniku King app member system. Macnica also identified 99 similar cases in 13 other countries and regions, although it said disclosure practices differ and it does not know whether Japan is the only target.

The reported methods include extracting API endpoints and keys from public smartphone apps, accessing internal API functions not available in app screens, abusing overly broad API permissions, and using stolen keys. JPCERT/CC also identified exploitation of CVE-2026-72898, an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in Metabase that can provide administrator access and expose credentials for connected databases. The center recommends patching affected Metabase versions, reviewing logs and account activity, rotating connected-database credentials, enforcing access controls and rate limits on every API endpoint, and limiting API-token privileges and lifetimes.

  • Attackers can extract API endpoints and keys from publicly released smartphone apps, then make requests that resemble normal app use while accessing functions not exposed through the app’s screens.
  • Of the 81 similar Japanese incidents disclosed since July, 65 contained too little detail to determine how attackers entered, limiting attribution of the current activity to any single method or group.
  • Metabase’s minimum safe releases are newer than the initial versions that fixed CVE-2026-72898, because the company later issued another critical advisory and raised its recommended baseline.
  • AhaSlides reported that an attacker accessed its Metabase environment from August 12 to September 7, showing that exploitation continued after the initial Metabase fix was released.
  • JPCERT/CC and Macnica caution that requests from listed source IP addresses are not proof of malicious activity because some may be shared VPN exit addresses; unusually heavy traffic or errors should instead prompt detailed log review.
Key Points
  • 01JPCERT/CC warned that attackers behind a series of personal-data leaks at Japanese organizations have abused mobile-app APIs, targeted known software flaws, and accessed business tools and employee systems that were not expected to be publicly reachable.
  • 02Macnica recorded 119 publicly disclosed, similar web-system personal-data theft or leak incidents in Japan through October 6, 2026, with 81 reported since July.
  • 03Park24 reported that data from about 6.6 million Times Car accounts was obtained by a third party, and that identity documents such as driver’s-license images leaked from about 1.6 million accounts.
  • 04JPCERT/CC identified exploitation of CVE-2026-72898, a critical unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in Metabase that can enable administrator access and theft of credentials for connected databases.
  • 05JPCERT/CC recommends access controls on every API endpoint, rate limits for abuse-prone functions, least-privilege API tokens, token expiration, and rapid token revocation.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a high-impact report of active exploitation and large-scale personal-data leaks in Japan, including abuse of mobile APIs and the critical, unauthenticated Metabase flaw CVE-2026-72898. It provides concrete indicators, affected-version guidance, compromise checks, and response steps relevant to organizations operating public APIs or Metabase.

    In plain words

    The United States and partner countries took control of websites supporting hacking tools used by Integrity Tech, a Chinese company linked to the Flax Typhoon campaign. The tools were used to look for weak points, send deceptive messages to gain access, and steal data from organizations including power companies, airports, universities, government bodies, health systems, and telecommunications providers. The case matters because Chinese government-linked hackers have sought quiet, long-term access to essential services, potentially allowing them to disrupt important functions later.

    Summary
    An international coalition led by U.S. agencies seized websites supporting Microscan and FishHub, tools used by China-linked Integrity Tech and Flax Typhoon to scan, phish, and compromise critical infrastructure worldwide.

    The U.S. Justice Department, working with international partners, seized websites supporting Microscan and FishHub, hacking tools operated by Beijing-based Integrity Tech. U.S. authorities said the company was hired by China’s Ministry of State Security and supplied China-linked threat actors with capabilities used against critical infrastructure and other organizations worldwide. The related advisory was supported by agencies in Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

    Microscan has reportedly been used since 2017 to identify specific weaknesses in websites, affecting organizations including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, and Taiwanese natural-gas and power entities. FishHub was designed to accelerate phishing campaigns and provide access after a network was breached; authorities said it was used against about 20 universities in Taiwan. The FBI, CISA, and NSA said these actors often target poorly monitored edge devices to maintain hidden, long-term access, while officials warned that Chinese government hackers may be positioning themselves in critical infrastructure networks for potential future disruption.

    • Integrity Tech’s role extended beyond conducting intrusions: authorities said it supplied scanning, phishing, botnet, and email-theft capabilities to China-linked threat actors, allowing malicious activity to operate at greater scale.
    • The threat actors reportedly favored edge devices that receive limited monitoring, using them to retain hidden, long-term access to victim networks.
    • Investigators found that some stolen email data was accessible only from IP addresses in Xiamen, China, indicating access controls were applied to the exfiltrated material.
    • The seizure follows a September 2024 disruption of a separate Mirai-based Flax Typhoon botnet involving more than 260,000 consumer devices, showing that Integrity Tech’s infrastructure has been the subject of repeated U.S. actions.
    Key Points
    • 01The U.S. Justice Department seized websites supporting Microscan and FishHub, tools created by Beijing-based Integrity Tech and used by China-linked threat actors.
    • 02Authorities said Microscan has been used since 2017 to scan websites for specific weaknesses, with targets including a South Carolina power company, Japanese and Polish airports, and Taiwanese natural-gas and power organizations.
    • 03FishHub was designed to speed up phishing operations and was used to provide remote access after a breach, including against about 20 universities in Taiwan.
    • 04The FBI, CISA, and NSA said Integrity Tech and related Chinese groups often target poorly monitored internet-facing devices to maintain long-term access to organizations.
    • 05The advisory was supported by Australia, Japan, the United Kingdom, Spain, New Zealand, and Canada, and described targeting across critical infrastructure and other sectors worldwide.

    In plain words

    The FBI and partner agencies say hackers linked to China-based Integrity Technology Group have broken into organizations since at least 2021 and stolen email, including from government offices, police, healthcare systems, schools, religious groups, and manufacturers. The targets span Southeast Asia, Africa, North America, and the United States, and the hackers reportedly ran a website that allowed other people to view stolen messages. This matters because private communications, account details, and information about important public services can be exposed or misused, affecting both organizations and the people they serve.

    Summary
    A joint FBI-led advisory says China-linked Integrity Technology Group actors have targeted organizations worldwide since at least 2021, stealing email and operating a portal that lets third parties access the stolen content. The group uses known vulnerabilities, password spraying, phishing-style XSS pages, and tools including SoftEther and Microsoft 365/Exchange email collectors.

    The FBI and agencies from six other countries said hackers linked to China-based Integrity Technology Group have targeted government organizations, law enforcement, healthcare systems, manufacturers, IT organizations, schools, and religious institutions since at least January 2021. Targets included organizations in Southeast Asia, Africa, and North America, as well as U.S. government services and critical sectors. In plain words

Bitdefender found harmful software already built into some cheap Android phones before buyers turn them on, meaning owners cannot normally remove it. The software can secretly add and delete apps, create fake advertising clicks for profit, gather information about the phone and its installed apps, and use the phone’s internet connection as part of a larger network controlled by criminals. Summary
Bitdefender uncovered Midnight Mimosa, a firmware-preinstalled Android malware family on low-cost MediaTek devices that operates with system privileges before a user ever turns the phone on. It can silently install payloads, evade Play Protect, conduct ad and click fraud, and enroll phones as residential-proxy botnet nodes; related ad-fraud apps were also found on Google Play.

Bitdefender identified Midnight Mimosa, a malware campaign preinstalled in the firmware of low-cost, multi-brand Android devices using MediaTek platforms. The persistent system applications appear under names including com.android.system.lite, com.android.sys.prot, and com.android.sys.gmsprot, and are present before the owner turns on the phone. Because they are platform-signed and run with system-level privileges, they cannot be normally uninstalled and can silently install or remove apps, grant permissions, and load code supplied remotely.

The malware uses hidden plugins and ordinary-looking cover apps, such as weather, app-lock, note, OCR, and icon tools, to generate fraudulent advertising impressions and clicks. It temporarily disables the Google Play Store before installing payloads, then re-enables it, and some samples falsely record Google Play as the installer despite lacking the Play-applied frosting signature block. Bitdefender observed the campaign on thousands of devices in more than 150 countries and found thirteen Google Play apps sharing related ad-fraud code and command servers. In addition to ad fraud, a dropped fake app-lock application can enroll devices as residential-proxy relay nodes, allowing operators to use victims’ internet connections as part of a remotely controlled network.

  • The malware can make sideloaded apps appear to have come from Google Play by recording com.android.vending as the installer, but Bitdefender notes that the absence of Google Play’s server-applied “frosting” signature block exposes the forged origin.
  • The operation rotates package names, signing certificates, native-library names, and payload versions, so Bitdefender recommends identifying the family through stable markers such as libeasy.so, cn.kw.lib.hex, and the api.weatherlive.world server rather than package-name blocklists.
  • The system component temporarily disables the Play Store immediately before installing a payload and re-enables it afterward, creating a window intended to prevent Play Protect from scanning the installation.
  • Because the root component resides in the phone’s system partition and is platform-signed, normal app removal is ineffective; the article says durable remediation requires firmware-level cleanup or disabling the component through ADB.
  • The campaign uses ordinary-looking weather, app-lock, note, and OCR apps as the visible advertising hosts, while separate hidden components supply the fraudulent click logic and control the timing remotely.

In plain words

Cisco warned that five serious software flaws could let an attacker take full control of certain Nexus network switches or force them to restart and disrupt network service. The affected equipment is Nexus 3000 and Nexus 9000 switches running standalone NX-OS, but only when particular optional features are turned on; Nexus 7000 devices and Nexus 9000 switches in ACI mode are not affected. Cisco has released updates and advises customers to install them or turn off unneeded features, because compromised or unavailable switches can interrupt the networks that depend on them.

Summary
Cisco issued patches for five critical NX-OS flaws that could let attackers gain root-level code execution or crash affected Nexus 3000 and 9000 switches when vulnerable features are enabled. Organizations should upgrade promptly or disable NX-API, NGOAM, and MPLS OAM where unnecessary.

Cisco released advisories for five critical vulnerabilities in NX-OS that could allow attackers to run code with root privileges on affected Nexus switches. If code execution is not achieved, the flaws can also crash processes and cause a device reload, producing a denial-of-service condition. Cisco said it was not aware of public announcements or malicious exploitation at the time the advisories were published.

The issues affect Nexus 3000 and Nexus 9000 Series switches running standalone NX-OS when NX-API, Next Generation OAM (NGOAM), or MPLS OAM is enabled. The NX-API issue can be triggered with a crafted HTTP request, while the NGOAM flaws involve crafted IP traffic and the MPLS OAM flaw involves a crafted MPLS echo-request packet. Nexus 7000 switches and Nexus 9000 devices in ACI mode are not affected, and Nexus 9000 systems with Silicon One ASICs are unaffected by the MPLS OAM issue.

Cisco recommends upgrading to fixed NX-OS releases identified through its Software Checker tool and disabling unneeded NX-API, NGOAM, or MPLS OAM features. For systems that cannot yet be upgraded and rebooted, Cisco provides temporary Live Protect shields. Cisco also released hardening updates for Cisco License, including flaws with severity scores up to 10.0, and recommends upgrading affected installations to version 10-202609 because no workarounds are available.

  • Exposure is configuration-dependent for the Nexus flaws: NX-API and MPLS OAM are disabled by default, while the NGOAM flaws require that feature to be enabled.
  • CVE-2026-76486 has additional prerequisites beyond NGOAM, requiring either SRv6 or a configured NV Overlay environment, while CVE-2026-76501 is limited to SRv6-enabled systems and only some Nexus 9000 models support SRv6.
  • Nexus 9000 switches using Silicon One ASICs are not affected by CVE-2026-76465 because they do not support the required MPLS OAM feature.
  • Cisco License has separate high- and critical-severity issues that affect vulnerable releases regardless of configuration, have no workarounds, and require an upgrade to version 10-202609; older Smart Software Manager releases will not be patched.
Key Points
  • 01Cisco disclosed five critical NX-OS vulnerabilities that can enable root-level arbitrary code execution on affected Nexus switches or cause processes to crash and devices to reload.
  • 02The flaws affect Nexus 3000 and Nexus 9000 Series switches in standalone NX-OS mode when NX-API, Next Generation OAM, or MPLS OAM is enabled.
  • 03Cisco said Nexus 7000 switches and Nexus 9000 switches operating in ACI mode are not affected by any of the five vulnerabilities.
  • 04Cisco recommends upgrading to fixed NX-OS releases, disabling unneeded affected features, or using temporary Live Protect shields when an upgrade and reboot cannot yet be performed.

In plain words

Researchers found a fake add-on for Terraform, a tool used by developers to manage cloud systems, that secretly installs spying and remote-control software on Mac, Linux, and Windows computers. The campaign is suspected to be linked to a North Korean group that has targeted cryptocurrency companies and Web3 developers. It can steal saved browser passwords, cookies that may keep people logged in, cryptocurrency wallet information, and other personal work data, while giving attackers ongoing access to the computer. This matters because a compromised developer tool can quietly put both the developer and the systems they help build at risk.

Summary
Zscaler researchers found a suspected North Korean TraderTraitor campaign using a trojanized Terraform provider to silently deliver FLATROOF and ROOFDECK malware to macOS, Linux, and Windows developer systems. The malware steals browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, and system information while establishing persistent remote access through resilient command-and-control channels.

Zscaler ThreatLabz reported a July 2026 campaign suspected to be linked to the North Korean TraderTraitor group that used a trojanized Terraform provider masquerading as an AWS provider. The provider executes malicious code when Terraform loads it but continues functioning normally, potentially making the compromise less noticeable. It downloads a Bash loader from a HashiCorp-themed lookalike domain and uses a temporary-directory lock file to limit repeated execution.

The loader selects payloads for macOS, Linux, or Windows based on the operating system and processor architecture, disguising encrypted executables as .woff font files. The resulting FLATROOF backdoor can establish persistence, receive commands through Telegram, GitHub, or an attacker-controlled HTTP service, and deploy Python scripts to steal browser data, shell history, system information, and cryptocurrency wallet-related data. A subsequent ROOFDECK backdoor can discover its control server through local configuration, a signed encrypted Pastebin entry, or Nostr profile metadata, and provides remote command execution, file operations, clipboard access, persistence controls, and other system-management capabilities.

  • The trojanized provider was designed to remain functional as a Terraform provider while launching its malicious routine, which could make the compromise less noticeable to users.
  • The loader disguises encrypted executables as font files, appending them after decoy font content and recovering them through a marker, Base64 decoding, and AES-256-CBC decryption.
  • The Bash loader can use Python, Node.js, Perl, or OpenSSL to decrypt its payload, allowing it to operate across systems with different installed software.
  • ROOFDECK verifies an RSA signature on the encrypted server address retrieved from Pastebin, preventing others from redirecting infected systems without the operator's signing key.
  • ROOFDECK can fall back to Nostr profile metadata to locate its Pastebin dead drop, providing another path for discovering its current control server.

  • 02The provider downloads a Bash loader from a HashiCorp-themed lookalike domain, and the loader selects encrypted FLATROOF payloads for macOS, Linux, or Windows based on the operating system and processor architecture.
  • 03FLATROOF is a Rust-based backdoor that supports Telegram, GitHub, and attacker-controlled HTTP channels for command-and-control, and includes platform-specific persistence methods.
  • 04FLATROOF deploys Python stealers that collect browser credentials, cookies, browsing data, command history, system details, and, on Windows, data associated with MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, and Rabby extensions.

In plain words

Cisco Talos found a campaign aimed at people connected to research organizations in Taiwan, using fake invitations to real or believable public events while pretending to represent trusted academic and policy institutions. The messages used polished, personalized wording, links that looked legitimate but led elsewhere, and altered event posters with harmful QR codes that could also trick people who only saw a printed copy. Victims were sent to a convincing fake Google sign-in page that could capture their password, extra sign-in approval, and access to their account. This matters because attackers can use trusted event details and realistic-looking webpages to take over accounts and spread the scam beyond the original email recipients.

Summary
Cisco Talos uncovered UAT-11985, a targeted campaign against Taiwanese research organizations that uses AI-assisted event invitations, tampered QR-code posters, and real-time Google adversary-in-the-middle phishing to steal credentials, MFA responses, and authenticated sessions.

Cisco Talos observed UAT-11985, a spear-phishing campaign targeting people affiliated with Taiwan-based research organizations in mid-2026. The actor impersonated institutions including the Taiwan European Union Centre, NCCU Institute of International Relations, and Taiwan Research Institute, using genuine or plausible public-event information to make invitation emails appear credible. Talos found that the purported senders were not confirmed as employees or representatives by the named organizations. The highly similar structure, broad professional flattery, and rapid topic-specific customization of the messages suggested likely AI-assisted content generation.

The emails used visible registration links that appeared legitimate, including Google Forms-style URLs, but redirected victims to actor-controlled phishing pages. The actor also altered QR codes on legitimate-looking event posters, potentially exposing people who encountered printed copies rather than the original emails. The malicious pages imitated Google Forms and then forced visitors to a spoofed Google sign-in flow offered in Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and English. Talos assessed with moderate confidence that the interface was originally authored in Simplified Chinese and later localized for the other languages.

The phishing kit functioned as a real-time relay between victims and Google authentication services, collecting account identifiers, passwords, browser details, and authentication challenges. It used HTTP POST requests to send captured information and a persistent WebSocket connection to receive instructions that controlled which sign-in or multi-factor authentication screen the victim saw. This design enabled the actor to mirror Google’s changing authentication flow and seek authenticated session tokens. Talos published ClamAV and Snort detection coverage and linked to indicators of compromise in its GitHub repository.

  • The campaign used genuine event details and visible Google Forms-style links as credibility signals while concealing redirects to phishing infrastructure, showing that accurate event information does not validate an invitation.
  • Altered QR codes on event posters could reach people beyond the original email recipients if the posters were printed or displayed, expanding the campaign from email into physical spaces.
  • The phishing framework separated captured-data uploads over HTTP from real-time instructions over WebSocket, allowing the fake page to track and reproduce Google’s changing sign-in and verification screens.
  • The phishing kit’s language design used Simplified Chinese as its base and default branch, with Traditional Chinese and English layered on afterward, which Talos cited as evidence that its interface was originally authored in Simplified Chinese.
Key Points
  • 01Cisco Talos observed UAT-11985, a spear-phishing campaign targeting individuals affiliated with Taiwan-based research organizations in mid-2026.
  • 02The campaign impersonated Taiwanese academic and policy institutions, reused legitimate event information, and used misleading registration links that redirected victims to actor-controlled phishing sites.
  • 03The actor attached legitimate-looking event posters with maliciously modified QR codes, creating an additional route to phishing pages for people who scanned the posters.
  • 04The phishing kit imitated Google sign-in pages in Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and English and used HTTP POST requests and WebSocket connections to relay authentication steps in real time.
  • 05Talos assessed with moderate confidence that the phishing kit’s interface was originally developed in Simplified Chinese before being adapted for Traditional Chinese and English.

Summary
The FakeGit campaign has reactivated, using 17,610 GitHub repositories to distribute SmartLoader and ultimately StealC malware through deceptive README download links. Its large pre-existing repository network and redundant hosted payloads make simple takedowns and blocklists ineffective.

The FakeGit campaign resumed activity on October 4 and now uses 17,610 GitHub repositories to distribute the SmartLoader malware, which can deliver other malware including the StealC infostealer. Apiiro reported that more than 13,000 repositories were pushed in 34 hours, peaking at 2,999 per hour. The operation uses mostly throwaway accounts, but researchers identified at least 700 accounts that appear to belong to legitimate developers. Similar activity has been observed since at least January, and FakeGit was linked to 7,600 malicious repositories in July.

The repositories use convincing README files with Download buttons that link to ZIP archives containing SmartLoader. Apiiro found that 97% of sampled commits changed only README files, while 88% redirected users to a ZIP file that installs SmartLoader. The campaign is difficult to disrupt because operators can repoint links to copies stored in forks, older files, release assets, issue attachments, and separate download-hosting repositories. Apiiro recommends checking repository owners, using official registries or vendor repositories for AI skills and MCP servers, and revoking GitHub sessions and access tokens if SmartLoader execution is suspected.

  • The operators did not need to create new repositories during the surge because they had already built a large repository fleet and only changed where the download links pointed.
  • Traditional blocking is limited because a domain-level block on a harmful file hosted on GitHub would also block GitHub itself, while 71% of the malicious repository fleet was not listed in URLhaus before Apiiro's report.
  • Removing a single malicious download link is insufficient because the same archive can be hosted through forks, older files, release assets, issue attachments, or separate download repositories.
  • At least 700 accounts used in the operation appeared to belong to legitimate developers, which can make repository-owner checks more difficult.
  • If SmartLoader may have run, Apiiro recommends treating it as a possible GitHub account compromise by revoking active sessions and access tokens and switching to passkeys.

  • 04The campaign can redirect download links to copies stored in forks, older files, release assets, issue attachments, and separate download-hosting repositories.
  • 05Apiiro recommends verifying repository owners and obtaining AI skills and MCP servers only from official registries or vendor repositories.

In plain words

Researchers found 16 fake Firefox add-ons that pretended to be Rabby or OKX cryptocurrency wallets and secretly collected the wallet recovery words and private keys people entered. Anyone who installed one and used it to import a real wallet could have their cryptocurrency stolen, even though the add-ons were removed by October 5, 2026. The case shows that browser add-ons that look like useful tools can be designed to monitor people or send their sensitive information to criminals, so users and organizations should remove add-ons they do not need.

Summary
Sixteen malicious Firefox extensions impersonated Rabby and OKX wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys during wallet-import flows, exfiltrating them to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers. Although Mozilla removed the extensions, anyone who entered wallet credentials should treat them as compromised and move assets to a newly created wallet from a clean system.

Cybersecurity researchers identified 16 malicious Mozilla Firefox extensions that impersonated Rabby Wallet and OKX Wallet. Four were Rabby Wallet clones and the remainder imitated OKX Wallet, presenting themselves as wallet portals, desktop utilities, or browser tools. During wallet-import processes, the extensions captured recovery phrases and private keys. They then attempted to send those secrets to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers infrastructure.

All but one of the identified add-ons contacted the *.icy-star-f45c.workers[.]dev domain. Researchers assessed the activity as a continuation of an earlier campaign documented in August 2026, with the operators changing package names, versions, extension IDs, descriptions, and appearances while reusing core wallet interfaces, credential-handling logic, and network infrastructure. The extensions had all been removed as of October 5, 2026. Users who entered a real recovery phrase or private key were advised to assume it was exposed, create a new wallet from a clean system, and move their assets.

The article also highlights other malicious or questionable Firefox, Chrome, and Edge extensions that can steal session cookies, collect browsing and social-media data, redirect users to cryptocurrency phishing pages, route traffic through proxies, or capture AI chatbot conversations. It recommends that users review and remove unnecessary browser extensions. Organizations are advised to audit extensions in managed environments and use runtime and behavior-based monitoring to detect suspicious activity.

  • The reported threat extends beyond cryptocurrency wallets: the article cites browser extensions that can steal Google session cookies, redirect users to wallet-phishing pages, route traffic through remotely supplied proxies, and collect AI chatbot conversations.
  • Organizations are advised to audit extensions in managed environments and use runtime and behavior-based monitoring to identify suspicious extension activity.

Two major South Korean megachurches, Yoido Full Gospel Church and SaRang Church, are investigating cyberattacks that may have exposed personal, financial and internal data belonging to hundreds of thousands of congregants and employees. Two major South Korean Protestant congregations, Yoido Full Gospel Church and SaRang Church, are investigating suspected cyberattacks that may have exposed sensitive member, employee, financial and internal information. Yoido Full Gospel Church said it identified a dataset containing personal information associated with approximately 850,000 members, while SaRang Church did not disclose the potential number affected. Both churches said they were taking steps with authorities and cybersecurity specialists to assess the incidents and prevent further harm.

Oasis Security analyzed files recovered from an overseas attacker-controlled server and described two separate intrusions that likely occurred in August. In one case, attackers installed a web shell to remotely control a compromised server, gained administrator-level access, and collected membership, payroll, accounting, internal-message and employee-login data. In the other, attackers used previously leaked passwords and flaws in internal applications to access unauthorized accounts and SAP software; the affected records included data associated with about 89,000 members and human-resources files for 286 employees. Researchers also found a technical connection to an earlier compromise of a U.S.-based Christian content platform and evidence that artificial intelligence was used during the intrusions.

  • The incidents involved two different paths into church systems: one attacker gained high-level server control through a web shell, while the other used leaked passwords and weaknesses in internal applications.

  • Researchers found that infrastructure used in these incidents had also been associated with an earlier compromise of a U.S.-based Christian content platform, indicating a technical connection between the events.
  • The suspected intrusions likely occurred in August, weeks before they became public, illustrating that unauthorized access can persist before an organization is alerted.

The U.S. State Department is offering up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of Zhang Yu, a Chinese national charged in the United States over alleged involvement in the 2021 HAFNIUM attacks on Microsoft Exchange Server. Zhang remains at large, and the charges against him have not been tested in court. The reward notice says he is wanted for alleged malicious cyber activities against U.S. critical infrastructure.

Zhang and Xu Zewei face a nine-count federal indictment alleging they coordinated hacking linked to China’s Shanghai State Security Bureau, part of the Ministry of State Security. The alleged activity included targeting U.S. universities and scientists working on COVID-19 vaccines, treatment, and testing, followed by exploitation of Microsoft Exchange Server flaws in the HAFNIUM campaign. Microsoft released fixes for four actively exploited zero-day flaws on March 2, 2021, and the FBI says the broader campaign compromised more than 12,700 U.S. organizations. Xu was arrested in Milan in July 2025 and extradited to the United States in April 2026.

In plain words

A reported Ukrainian drone strike forced Yandex to shut down a data center in Sasovo, Russia, causing problems for its online cloud services and products such as Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents. Some Russian websites also became unavailable, although Yandex moved work to other facilities and said they were operating normally with some limits. The event shows that strikes on facilities holding computers and data can disrupt everyday internet services far beyond the immediate target, as Russia and Ukraine both face damage to digital infrastructure during the war.

Summary
A reported Ukrainian drone strike disrupted a Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, causing a major outage affecting Yandex Cloud and related services before workloads were moved to other facilities.

A reported Ukrainian drone strike disrupted a Yandex data center in Sasovo, in Russia’s Ryazan region, prompting the company to shut down the facility. Yandex acknowledged a power outage but did not publicly connect it to the drone strike, and no injuries were reported. Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses intercepted Ukrainian drones over Ryazan and other regions, while local authorities reported no damage and Ukraine’s military did not comment.

Yandex said it moved workloads to other data centers, which were functioning normally, although customers could face limits when creating new cloud resources. NetBlocks reported Yandex network connectivity fell to roughly 70% of normal levels, and the outage reportedly affected Yandex Cloud, Yandex Disk, Yandex Documents, and several Russian websites. The incident comes amid continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, which Ukrainian officials say they are addressing by moving equipment underground, transferring data to cloud services, and relocating some infrastructure abroad.

  • Yandex’s ability to move workloads to other facilities limited the outage, but the remaining restriction on creating new cloud resources shows that failover did not fully restore service capacity.
  • The disruption affected services beyond the data center itself, including Yandex Disk, Yandex Documents, and unrelated Russian websites that depended on Yandex infrastructure.
  • The affected data center was reportedly housed at a machine-tool plant sanctioned by the United Kingdom for links to Russia’s defense sector, while the intended target remains unclear.
  • Ukraine has described resilience measures including moving equipment underground, using cloud services, and relocating some infrastructure abroad in response to Russian strikes on digital facilities.
Key Points
  • 01A reported Ukrainian drone strike disrupted a Yandex data center in Sasovo, in Russia's Ryazan region, on Thursday, though Yandex did not publicly attribute the outage to the strike.
  • 02Yandex said it moved workloads to other facilities, but warned that customers could face limits when creating new resources in its cloud infrastructure.
  • 03NetBlocks reported that Yandex network connectivity fell to about 70% of normal levels, while Russian media reported disruption to Yandex Cloud, Yandex Disk, Yandex Documents, and several websites.
  • 04Russia's Defense Ministry said it intercepted Ukrainian drones over several regions including Ryazan, while local authorities reported no damage and Ukraine's military did not publicly comment.
  • 05The disruption occurred amid continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, including attacks that reportedly damaged at least six Ukrainian data centers late last month.

Summary
Empire Market co-creator Raheim Hamilton was sentenced to 40 years in U.S. federal prison for operating the dark-web marketplace, which facilitated roughly $430 million in illegal transactions, primarily drug sales, between 2018 and 2020.

Raheim Hamilton, also known as “Sydney” and “ZeroAngel,” was sentenced to 40 years in U.S. federal prison for co-creating and operating Empire Market. The dark-web marketplace facilitated more than 4 million transactions and about $430 million in illegal sales between 2018 and 2020. Hamilton operated the site with co-defendant Thomas Pavey, who pleaded guilty to a federal drug conspiracy charge and is scheduled to be sentenced later.

Empire Market was accessible through Tor and was modeled on AlphaBay, selling drugs, counterfeit currency, stolen account credentials, hacking tools, and personal information. Drug sales accounted for nearly $375 million, and the site had roughly 1.68 million registered users at its August 2020 peak. Transactions were limited to cryptocurrency, while users were encouraged to use transaction-masking services and encrypted messages to conceal activity.

U.S. investigators made undercover purchases from the site and intercepted a package containing methamphetamine ordered through Empire Market. Authorities said they had seized $75 million in cryptocurrency during the investigation. Hamilton agreed to forfeit three Virginia properties, about 1,230 bitcoin, and 24.4 Ether.

  • Empire Market was built to resemble AlphaBay and had grown to roughly 1.68 million registered users by August 2020, including more than 5,000 vendors.
  • The operators went beyond hosting listings by employing moderators to resolve buyer-seller disputes, with Hamilton supervising about five moderators and sometimes handling disputes himself.
  • The marketplace encouraged sellers to earn better ratings by concealing drug shipments effectively, linking its vendor-rating system to evasion of detection.
  • Investigators supported the case with undercover purchases and an intercepted package, in addition to seizing $75 million in cryptocurrency.
  • Hamilton’s forfeiture agreement included real estate and approximately 1,230 bitcoin and 24.4 Ether, showing that the case targeted assets as well as imprisonment.

In plain words

Four senior employees at a multinational consumer goods company received fake document-sharing emails that appeared to come from their own employer. The sender used a stolen email account at one Korean company to send mail as a different company, allowing the messages to pass common email safety checks and reach inboxes. The link tested whether recipients were already signed in to Microsoft, helping criminals identify real, active accounts before potentially creating a more convincing password-stealing page. This matters because trustworthy-looking emails can come from legitimate email services, so people and organizations need to scrutinize unexpected internal document requests rather than relying only on automated filters.

Summary
A phishing campaign used a stolen credential on a shared Korean email platform to send an SPF-passing document-share lure impersonating recipients’ own employer. An X-Authinfo header exposed the cross-company authenticated account, while the link performed a Microsoft silent identity probe rather than directly stealing mailbox tokens.

A document-sharing phishing lure targeted four senior legal and commercial employees at a multinational coffee and consumer goods group between November 18 and December 2, 2025. The messages impersonated each recipient’s own employer, claimed a contract required a signature, and presented a secure folder supposedly restricted to the recipient’s company domain. All four messages were quarantined, and an analyst marked the sender as malicious.

A provider-added X-Authinfo header showed that a mailbox at one Korean company authenticated the SMTP session while the email was sent as an address at an unrelated Korean company, from a Microsoft Azure IP address. The shared business-mail host was authorized to send for the impersonated domain, allowing SPF to pass despite the apparent credential compromise; the message had no DKIM signature and received dmarc=bestguesspass and compauth=pass. Its link routed through an abused marketing platform to Microsoft’s authorization endpoint with prompt=none and only basic identity scopes, making it a silent check for an active Microsoft session rather than mailbox-token theft. The article recommends searching for X-Authinfo mismatches between the authenticating account and the visible From address, and treating unexpected internal document-sharing requests as a distinct phishing pattern.

  • The provider-added X-Authinfo header can expose a mismatch between the account used to log in for sending and the address shown to recipients, providing evidence of a compromised account even when the message passes standard sender checks.
  • A shared email host can let a stolen credential inherit authorization to send for multiple customer domains, so SPF confirms an approved sending route rather than the legitimacy of the person using the account.
  • The Microsoft sign-in link used only basic identity permissions and no long-term, mail, or Graph permissions, making it an account and session reconnaissance step rather than evidence of mailbox-access token theft.
  • Rendering a familiar logo as colored HTML table cells instead of an image can evade checks that identify brand impersonation by analyzing or matching image files.
  • Footer links retained a previous victim’s email address and organization identifier inside encoded tracking parameters, showing that reused phishing templates can leak useful campaign artifacts that ordinary body-text searches may miss.
Key Points
  • 01A phishing lure targeting four senior mailboxes at a multinational consumer goods group used an X-Authinfo header showing that an account at one Korean company authenticated SMTP delivery for a From address at an unrelated Korean company.
  • 02The message passed SPF through a shared business-mail host, had no DKIM signature, and was delivered to the Inbox with Microsoft authentication results including dmarc=bestguesspass and compauth=pass.
  • 03The lure impersonated each recipient’s own employer, presented a document requiring a signature, and used a Microsoft-style four-square logo rendered as colored HTML table cells rather than an image.
  • 04Its authorize link used Microsoft’s OAuth endpoint with prompt=none and only openid, profile, and email scopes, which the article describes as a silent identity and active-session check rather than mailbox token theft.
  • 05All four messages were quarantined, and the article recommends searching mail stores for X-Authinfo mismatches between the authenticating account and the From address.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete phishing campaign analysis with a particularly actionable X-Authinfo header artifact that can reveal cross-company SMTP credential misuse even when SPF passes. The dataset reportedly includes roughly 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and sensitive payroll, tax, contract, and timecard records.

More than 100 members of Congress sent a letter to Google and Spirit Airlines asking them to halt a proposed $10 million deal to provide Google with internal Spirit data for AI-model training. The letter, led by Rep. Steven Horsford and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, was signed by 114 federal lawmakers. Google has said the data would be deidentified before transfer.

The proposed sale reportedly includes about 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages, employment contracts, timecard records, and payroll and tax information. Lawmakers warned that removing names, email addresses, and other direct identifiers may not make the dataset anonymous, particularly in the context of modern AI. They asked the companies to seek former employees’ input, exclude as much employee information as possible, limit the data’s use, and conduct an independent employee confidentiality review. Spirit announced plans to shut down in May, with nearly 1,000 people losing jobs in Las Vegas.

  • The proposed AI-training dataset reportedly combines communications, workplace chat, contracts, attendance records, and payroll and tax information, creating a much broader employee-data collection than a single business system alone.

  • The requested safeguards go beyond data scrubbing: lawmakers called for former employee feedback, minimizing the employee data transferred, limits on future use, and an independent confidentiality review.
  • The privacy dispute concerns a company that is shutting down, with nearly 1,000 job losses reported in Las Vegas, where parts of Rep. Steven Horsford’s district are located.

A Maryland man, 36-year-old Jonathan Spalletta, was convicted of stealing more than $53 million from decentralized cryptocurrency exchange Uranium Finance in two April 2021 hacks. Prosecutors said the thefts drained most of the exchange’s holdings and forced it to shut down. Spalletta faces up to 10 years in prison for computer fraud and up to 20 years for money laundering.

In the first breach, Spalletta used a flaw in Uranium’s smart-contract code to issue zero-token withdrawal commands and take about \(1.4 million from a liquidity pool. He then obtained a nearly \)386,000 sham bug bounty from the stolen funds in exchange for returning the remainder. Three weeks later, he exploited a separate transaction-verification error involving 1,000 instead of 10,000, enabling him to withdraw nearly 90% of pooled assets while depositing effectively zero tokens.

The article says Spalletta laundered stolen cryptocurrency through Tornado Cash and multiple decentralized exchanges. Authorities recovered roughly $31 million in cryptocurrency and seized collectibles purchased with proceeds, including Magic: The Gathering and Pokémon items and an ancient Roman coin. Crypto fraud investigator ZachXBT had linked more than 11,200 ETH withdrawn from Tornado Cash to the Uranium hacker in December 2023.

  • Although the funds were moved through Tornado Cash and decentralized exchanges, investigators linked more than 11,200 ETH withdrawn from Tornado Cash to the Uranium Finance hacker and authorities later recovered roughly $31 million in cryptocurrency.

Ajay Shinjin, 25, was sentenced to two and a half years in prison at Inner London Crown Court for his role in a cryptocurrency theft scheme. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation and transferring criminal property. Police said the scheme stole nearly $260,000 in cryptocurrency from four victims in November 2021. Shinjin used proceeds to fund luxury holidays in Dubai and buy gold-plated dental grills.

The criminals took control of victims’ phone numbers by moving them to SIM cards they controlled, then intercepted text-message security codes to enter bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets. BT detected unauthorized customer-number transfers and provided data that helped police identify several suspects, including Shinjin, who was linked to four eSIM-capable devices. Investigators traced about £27,000 from one victim and the full £17,000 stolen from another victim to Shinjin’s cryptocurrency wallet. City of London Police said the case demonstrated that people using technology to commit financial fraud would be brought to justice.

  • Control of a victim’s phone number enabled the criminals to bypass text-message account protections because they could receive the one-time codes sent to that number.

Talos found these methods steered AI verdicts in an attacker’s favor about 35 percent of the time.

Talos says the MANTLEMAZE family combines AI-focused deception with abuse of vulnerable drivers to disable endpoint detection and response software from kernel space. Because the misleading instructions must be written in plaintext, Talos recommends that defenders flag imperative language aimed at analysis systems and ensure extracted sample text is treated as evidence rather than as a directive.

    The newsletter also emphasizes intentional risk management for legacy systems that cannot be updated without disrupting essential operations. Its example describes isolating outdated check-printing devices onto a separate network with no internet access, reducing both exposure and the chance that attackers would find the devices during internal mapping. The article argues that such compensating controls can help keep critical services running while reducing risk from unsupported software and hardware.

In plain words

Researchers found that some malicious programs now contain hidden written messages aimed at confusing AI tools that help inspect suspicious files. These messages try to persuade the tool that the file is harmless, protected by copyright, or should not be examined, even when the program is dangerous. This matters to organizations that use AI to help spot threats, because attackers are adapting to those defenses; however, the messages must remain readable in the file and can be detected if tools treat them as evidence rather than commands.

Summary
Cisco Talos finds malware authors increasingly embedding plaintext prompt-injection strings to manipulate AI-assisted malware analysis, but the simplest direct instructions only inconsistently steer models and are readily detectable. Defenders should treat all text extracted from samples as untrusted evidence rather than executable instructions.

Cisco Talos describes “AI-analysis evasion,” in which malware embeds natural-language text intended to influence AI systems used to triage or analyze suspicious files. It tracked 84 samples from January 2025 through July 2026 across FRUITSHELL, PLOTSAFE, HOLLOWCLAD, and MANTLEMAZE. The technique targets the stage where text is extracted from a file and passed to a language model, rather than conventional binary-analysis defenses such as packing or anti-debugging checks.

FRUITSHELL used comments falsely claiming it only generated prime numbers, while PLOTSAFE generated varied versions of similar claims and used a dummy Go function to preserve the strings. HOLLOWCLAD and MANTLEMAZE placed instructions in multiple AI chat-template formats and added misleading copyright, government-contract, certification, and other intimidation claims. Talos’ testing found that simple direct instructions were the most consistently effective at steering model conclusions, although results were mixed overall and more complex techniques could make models more suspicious. Because the messages must be plaintext to work, Talos recommends detecting such imperative language and ensuring extracted sample text is treated as evidence, never as instruction.

  • The least sophisticated approach—plain-language instructions telling an AI not to analyze a file—was more effective in Talos testing than more elaborate template spraying and intimidation content, which sometimes made models more suspicious.
  • FRUITSHELL’s two-line message was reused verbatim by at least four distinct actors in nine later scripts, including more capable tooling with AMSI bypasses and runtime compilation, showing that this technique spread independently of overall malware sophistication.
  • PLOTSAFE’s author added a 29-byte unused function solely to keep the anti-analysis text from being removed by the Go compiler, demonstrating that the evasion strings were deliberately engineered rather than incidental comments.
  • Because these evasion messages must remain readable inside a sample to reach an AI analysis pipeline, they create a persistent detection opportunity for defenders despite their potential to influence model output.

  • 04HOLLOWCLAD and MANTLEMAZE used multiple AI chat-template formats to try to match the format used by an analysis system, while also including misleading claims intended to deter analysis.

In plain words

Elastic introduced AlertZero, a new feature for security teams that helps sort through large numbers of warnings and connect related signs of possible wrongdoing. It can investigate suspicious activity, look for threats, suggest improvements to security rules, and recommend actions such as disconnecting a computer from a network, while people can choose how much authority to give it. This matters because security teams can miss important problems when too many warnings arrive too quickly, especially as attackers use AI to increase their activity.

Summary
Elastic announced AlertZero, an agentic Elastic Security layer designed to reduce alert backlogs by automating triage, threat hunting, detection tuning, and endpoint forensics. Its configurable Watches provide evidence-backed proposed actions while retaining analyst control over consequential decisions.

Elastic introduced AlertZero, an agentic layer for Elastic Security intended to help security operations teams work toward answering every alert in their queue. It addresses high alert volumes by correlating and enriching activity at scale, reducing false positives, proposing actions, and helping create and tune detections. AlertZero uses agents called Watches, which are organized around Triage, Hunt, Detection, and Forensics responsibilities.

Watches run on triggers or schedules and produce evidence-backed Proposed Actions that analysts can approve, modify, escalate, or dismiss. Teams can configure each Worker for manual, assisted, or supervised operation, although consequential actions are presented for analyst approval according to the stated controls. In the article’s example, AlertZero linked an impossible-travel login for an executive account with endpoint evidence of an unsigned process accessing browser session material, then proposed host isolation through Elastic Defend.

Beyond triage, the Hunt Watch uses threat research and available telemetry to look for evidence of relevant threats, while the Detection Watch examines recurring false positives and coverage gaps to prepare proposed rule changes. Detection proposals can include the existing and suggested logic, motivating alerts, diagnosis, and backtest results, but analysts still need to validate that changes preserve detection of known malicious activity. Elastic states that AlertZero supports proprietary and open-source models across Elastic Cloud, self-managed deployments, and fully air-gapped environments.

  • AlertZero Watches do not operate as a mandatory sequence, so a hunt can begin from threat research and detection tuning can begin from recurring false-positive closures without an initial alert.
  • The same investigation record can combine suspicious sign-in evidence, endpoint behavior, related alerts, affected entities, follow-up questions, and a recommended response, reducing the need to hand work between separate tools or teams.
  • Detection-rule tuning proposals include both the current and suggested logic plus backtest results, but the article stresses that removing benign samples is not sufficient proof that malicious activity will still be detected.
  • Autonomy is controlled separately for individual tasks, allowing teams to automate routine triage while retaining human review for higher-impact decisions such as changing detection rules or isolating systems.
  • AlertZero is designed to support proprietary and open-source AI models across Elastic Cloud, self-managed deployments, and fully air-gapped environments.
Key Points
  • 01Elastic introduced AlertZero as an agentic layer for Elastic Security intended to help security operations teams work toward answering every alert.
  • 02AlertZero includes four Watches—Triage, Hunt, Detection, and Forensics—that perform distinct tasks and can run on triggers or schedules.
  • 03Watches produce evidence-backed Proposed Actions that analysts can approve, modify, escalate, or dismiss, with autonomy configurable for each Worker.

Act Before the Incident: Process-Aware Policy in Your SWG
