35
In plain words

Netskope has added information about which program made an internet request, and which program started it, to its web-security service. This helps companies spot and stop suspicious scripts or unapproved apps before they connect online, rather than discovering them only after they have run on an employee’s device. It matters because automated AI-driven activity can make huge numbers of requests quickly and may hide data theft or other harmful actions among normal web traffic.

Summary
Netskope says its Client now sends process and parent-process details to its Next-Gen Secure Web Gateway, enabling real-time policies and logging to identify and block suspicious application traffic before it can access the internet.

Netskope says its Client now provides process names and parent process names to the Netskope One Next-Gen Secure Web Gateway (NG-SWG). This information is available for real-time policy controls and transaction logging. The company positions the capability as a way to stop suspicious scripts and applications before they make internet requests, rather than relying only on endpoint tools that act after a process is already running.

The added context can be used in Real-Time Protection and SSL do-not-decrypt policies, including rules that trigger when processes such as curl.exe or parent processes such as powershell.exe are detected. Netskope says process data can also help investigate suspicious activity, including transfers of source code to personal cloud storage and unusual traffic that normally bypasses inspection for employee privacy. The article also highlights dedicated egress IP addresses, application instance awareness, and real-time user coaching as additional NG-SWG policy capabilities.

  • Web requests related to personal finances or health may be bypassed to protect employee privacy, but the article notes that this can create a covert channel that AI could exploit; process context can help identify unusual programs generating that traffic.
  • Process and parent-process records can support investigations into apparent data theft by helping determine whether a user may have been targeted by unknown prompts, scripts, or processes that moved data to compromised personal cloud storage.
  • Real-time user coaching can collect a user’s justification and permit a transaction instead of simply blocking it, creating feedback that can be used to refine security policies.
  • Application instance awareness can distinguish company and personal versions of cloud applications, allowing organizations to review transfers of company data to personal storage accounts, including when an employee leaves.
Key Points
  • 01Netskope Client now sends process names and parent process names to the Netskope One Next-Generation Secure Web Gateway for real-time policy controls and logging.
  • 02The added process context can allow policies to act before a subsequent process runs, rather than relying solely on endpoint tools that terminate a risky process after it is already running.
  • 03Real-Time Protection and SSL do-not-decrypt policies can be configured to trigger when a specific process, such as curl.exe, or parent process, such as powershell.exe, is detected.
  • 04Process and parent process names are available in Netskope Transaction Events to help identify which application on a device generated a request.
  • 05Netskope also highlights dedicated egress IP addresses, application instance awareness, and real-time user coaching as other Next-Generation Secure Web Gateway policy capabilities.

OAuth grants pile up faster than you can review them. Here's how to keep up.

TAGScontext-aigoogle-workspacemcpmicrosoft-365microsoft-teamsnudge-securityoauthoauth-grant-risk-analystslackvercel
25
In plain words

The article says employees often click “Allow” to connect work apps to services such as calendars, email, chat, files, or code, creating permissions that can remain active long after the original decision. It says this affects organizations whose employees use many third-party apps, and points to a Vercel breach linked to a compromised access token from Context.ai. The broader risk is that forgotten or overly broad app connections can give outsiders a path to sensitive company data, so the sponsored article promotes Nudge Security as a way to find, assess, and remove them.

Summary
Sponsored by Nudge Security, the article argues that organizations need dedicated OAuth grant discovery, risk assessment, and lifecycle governance because grants can remain active outside traditional SSO controls. It promotes Nudge Security’s AI-driven OAuth Grant Risk Analyst to prioritize, review, and help revoke risky app connections at scale.

The sponsored article argues that employee-approved OAuth grants create persistent connections between third-party applications and corporate data, often outside normal single sign-on and multi-factor authentication controls. It says these grants can remain valid while dormant and may not appear in activity logs, making them difficult for IT and security teams to inventory and review. The article cites the Vercel breach as involving a compromised OAuth token from Context.ai that had been connected to an employee’s enterprise Google Workspace account.

Nudge Security says its platform discovers OAuth grants, app-to-app integrations, API keys, service accounts, and remote MCP server connections across an organization’s SaaS environment. Its OAuth Grant Risk Analyst evaluates the grantor, vendor security posture, permissions, and accessible data, then recommends that a grant be permitted, justified, or revoked. The article says security teams retain approval over actions, while Nudge can send justification requests, alert on new OAuth activity, and revoke risky or unused grants, including during employee offboarding.

  • OAuth access does not automatically inherit the protections of single sign-on or multi-factor authentication, so organizations need a separate process to review and manage these app permissions.
  • Dormant app permissions can remain valid without generating activity logs, meaning a review process based only on observed use can miss potentially active access paths.
  • Even “Sign in with Google” connections may create identity-only grants that should be included in an organization’s inventory alongside more visibly active integrations.
  • The article argues that manual review does not scale because a single thorough grant review can take about 45 minutes, while its promoted analysis agent is claimed to produce a recommendation in 15 seconds.
  • Assessing a grant requires considering the employee who approved it, the app provider, the permissions requested, and the data the app can reach, rather than relying only on a general risk score.
Key Points
  • 01OAuth grants create continuing connections between apps and corporate data, and the article says they can remain valid even after an employee’s credentials are disabled in some circumstances.
  • 02The article states that a 1,000-person company could have roughly 88,000 OAuth grants, including about 31,000 with permissions to access data, based on Nudge Security figures.
  • 03The article cites the recent Vercel breach as involving a compromised OAuth token from Context.ai, an AI tool connected to an employee’s enterprise Google Workspace account.
  • 04Nudge Security says its platform discovers OAuth grants, API keys, service accounts, and remote MCP server connections across an organization’s SaaS environment.
  • 05The sponsored article says Nudge Security’s OAuth Grant Risk Analyst evaluates grants and recommends that organizations permit, justify, or revoke them, while leaving final action approval to the security team.

This is a sponsored, evergreen product-marketing article about OAuth grant governance rather than reporting a new incident or urgent vulnerability. It may be useful background for teams managing SaaS access, but it does not provide actionable details about a current threat.

deception technique

An AI language-model product referenced in security reporting.
default branch concept

defenders concept

deleted concept
Deleted means removed from normal access, though copies may sometimes still exist in backups, logs, or recovery areas.

denial-of-service attacks technique

denial-of-service condition concept
A denial-of-service condition is a situation where a system becomes unavailable or unusable for legitimate users.
denmark other
Denmark is a country in Northern Europe.

A software protection and anti-tampering technology sometimes referenced in misleading malware labels.

The main U.S. federal law enforcement agency responsible for prosecuting federal crimes and upholding justice.
dependencies concept

dependency concept

detection concept

Detection and analysis is the incident-response phase where teams identify alerts and determine what happened.
detection rule concept
A detection rule is a set of instructions a security tool uses to spot suspicious activity or known threats.
detection rules concept
Detection rules are instructions security tools use to flag suspicious behavior or known attack patterns.
Detection Signals concept
Alerts or indicators sent by a system when it finds something suspicious.
detection signatures concept
Detection signatures are patterns that security tools use to recognize known malware, attacks, or suspicious behavior.

detections concept

developer accounts concept

developer environments concept
Developer environments are the computers, tools, accounts, and code repositories programmers use to build software.

disruption concept

Dynamo is a product or target platform referenced in security reporting.

The protection of workers' personal information from unnecessary collection, sharing, or exposure.

encrypted communications concept

encrypted data concept

encryption concept
Encryption is a way of scrambling information so only someone with the right key can read it.

safeguards concept

scanner tool

scanning technique

scans concept

screenshots concept

Security Codes concept
Temporary codes used to verify a person's identity during sign-in or account recovery.
Security flaws concept
Weaknesses or mistakes in software or systems that attackers may be able to exploit.
Security incidents concept

security policies concept

security posture concept

security products concept
Software or hardware designed to protect systems from cyber threats, like antivirus or firewalls.
security professionals concept

security teams concept

security testing concept
Security testing is checking software, systems, or networks to find weaknesses before attackers can exploit them.
security tools tool

self-managed deployments concept

sender concept
